#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP)
Description: The Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP) is a nationally representative longitudinal survey that provides comprehensive information on the dynamics of income, employment, household composition, and government program participation. SIPP is also a leading source of data on economic well-being, family dynamics, education, wealth, health insurance, child care, and food security. The survey interviews individuals for several years and provides monthly data about changes in household and family composition and economic circumstances over time.
URL: https://census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp.html

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

[Federal Register Volume 91, Number 151 (Friday, August 7, 2026)]
[Notices]
[Pages 51147-51148]
From the Federal Register Online via the Government Publishing Office [www.gpo.gov]
[FR Doc No: 2026-16188]


=======================================================================
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE

Census Bureau


Agency Information Collection Activities; Submission to the 
Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for Review and Approval; Comment 
Request; Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP)

AGENCY: U.S. Census Bureau, Commerce.

ACTION: Notice of information collection, request for comment.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

SUMMARY: The Department of Commerce, in accordance with the Paperwork 
Reduction Act (PRA) of 1995, invites the general public and other 
Federal agencies to comment on proposed and continuing information 
collections. These comments help us assess the impact of our 
information collection requirements and minimize the public's reporting 
burden. The purpose of this notice is to allow for 60 days of public 
comment on the proposed revision of the Survey of Income and Program 
Participation (SIPP), prior to the submission of the information 
collection request (ICR) to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) 
for approval.

DATES: To ensure consideration, comments regarding this proposed 
information collection must be received on or before October 6, 2026.

ADDRESSES: Interested persons are invited to submit written comments by 
email to [email protected]. Please reference SIPP OMB Comments in 
the subject line of your comments. You may also submit comments, 
identified by Docket Number USBC-2026-0364, to the Federal e-Rulemaking 
Portal: http://www.regulations.gov. All comments received are part of 
the public record. No comments will be posted to http://www.regulations.gov for public viewing until after the comment period 
has closed. Comments will generally be posted without change. All 
Personally Identifiable Information (for example, name and address) 
voluntarily submitted by the commenter may be publicly accessible. Do 
not submit Confidential Business Information or otherwise sensitive or 
protected information. You may submit attachments to electronic 
comments in Microsoft Word, Excel, or Adobe PDF file formats.

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: Requests for additional information or 
specific questions related to collection activities should be directed 
to Sharon Stern, Assistant Division Chief and SIPP Program Director, 
301-763-5638, [email protected].

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

I. Abstract

    The U.S. Census Bureau plans to request clearance from the Office 
of Management and Budget (OMB) for a field test of the Survey of Income 
and Program Participation (SIPP) in calendar year 2027. This collection 
will be in lieu of a national collection using the questionnaires, 
systems, and processes in place since 2014.
    Since 1983, SIPP has been the primary source of information about 
annual and sub-annual dynamics of income, families and households, 
movement into and out of government programs, and interactions of these 
topics in a single, unified dataset

[[Page 51148]]

allowing for in-depth, informed analyses. Government domestic policy 
formulators and evaluators depend heavily upon the information 
collected in the SIPP in their analyses of the distribution of income 
received either directly as money or indirectly as in-kind benefits and 
the effect of tax and transfer programs on that distribution. They also 
rely on the SIPP data to provide improved and expanded information on 
the dynamics of income and the general economic and financial situation 
of the U.S. population in the context of the household situation. The 
SIPP has measured levels of economic well-being and permitted 
measurement of sub-annual and annual changes in these levels over time.
    Since the inception of the program, SIPP has been an interviewer-
administered household-based survey. Each panel featured a nationally 
representative sample of addresses whose household members were 
interviewed either in person or over the phone several times over a 
multi-year period. In recent years, SIPP has been researching new 
methods to mitigate concerns related to increasing costs for 
interviewer-administered surveys, declining response rates among 
sampled addresses, and increasing attrition of responding households in 
subsequent panels.
    At the forefront of SIPP modernization efforts is the adoption of a 
self-administered internet survey as the primary mode for data 
collection with targeted in-person interviewing of a select number of 
non-responding households. The addition of a SIPP self-response mode is 
one element of a larger, bureau-wide effort to modernize data 
collection systems.
    As SIPP is the premier source of comprehensive information on the 
dynamics of income, employment, household composition, and government 
program participation, testing the impact of the multi-mode data 
collection, statistical methods improvements, and agency-wide 
collection and processing systems is critical. The Census Bureau is 
implementing a multi-year testing strategy. In the summer of 2026, the 
Census Bureau is conducting an internet self-response field test using 
a subset of the redesigned SIPP instrument items on a national sample 
to assess the feasibility of a self-administered data collection (OMB 
number 0607-0978).
    The goals of the 2027 SIPP field test are to build upon the 2026 
test by adding content to the questionnaire; introducing a multi-mode 
survey that incorporates both self-response and non-response computer 
assisted personal interviewing (CAPI); introducing alternative sample 
and weighting methodologies; and using the Census Bureau's Business 
Ecosystem entities for all aspects of the survey process. We will use 
the test to evaluate the frame, sample, weighting, and non-response 
bias; to demonstrate the application of the new systems and processes 
to the SIPP design; research additional opportunities to reduce 
respondent burden through the use of administrative data systems; and 
to assess the quality of key estimates using the new methodologies. The 
2027 SIPP field test will be an important step toward building the 
modern program.
    The design of the test survey is purposefully scalable, as the 
future SIPP design is expected to be. The sample size listed in this 
notice is based on initial budget estimates and allows for expansion. 
The multi-mode data collection vision for the SIPP program includes a 
dual-sample design. One part of the sample will be invited to respond 
through a web-mode instrument only. The second sample component will be 
invited to self-respond on the internet. Among that group, non-
respondents will be contacted for in-person interviews.

II. Method of Collection

    The 2027 SIPP will use a web instrument for both the internet Self-
Response (ISR) and the CAPI modes of data collection. All sampled 
households will receivemail invitations to complete the survey online. 
To increase sample representativeness, field representatives will be 
sent to a small number of nonresponding ISR cases to administer the 
survey in person. The redesigned SIPP interview consists of one adult 
answering questions about each member of the household and uses a six-
month reference period. In instances where the residence is not 
accessible or the respondent makes a request, the field representative 
may conduct the interview by telephone.

III. Data

    OMB Control Number: 0607-1000.
    Form Number(s): SIPP ISR Web Instrument (no form number), SIPP 
nonresponse follow-up CAPI electronic instrument (no form number).
    Type of Review: Regular submission, New Information Collection 
Request.
    Affected Public: Individuals or households.
    Estimated Number of Respondents: 6,000.
    Estimated Time per Response: 40 minutes to respond to survey and 10 
total minutes for reading contact materials.
    Estimated Number of Non-Respondents: 14,000.
    Estimated Time per Non-response: 10 minutes.
    Estimated Total Annual Burden Hours: We estimate 5,000 burden hours 
from those responding to the survey and 2,334 burden hours from 
households that do not respond to the survey for a total of 7,334 
hours.
    Estimated Total Annual Cost to Public: $0 (This is not the cost of 
respondents' time, but the indirect costs respondents may incur for 
such things as purchases of specialized software or hardware needed to 
report, or expenditures for accounting or records maintenance services 
required specifically by the collection.)
    Respondent's Obligation: Voluntary.
    Legal Authority: Title 13, United States Code, Sections 141 and 
182.

IV. Request for Comments

    We are soliciting public comments to permit the Department/Bureau 
to: (a) Evaluate whether the proposed information collection is 
necessary for the proper functions of the Department, including whether 
the information will have practical utility; (b) Evaluate the accuracy 
of our estimate of the time and cost burden for this proposed 
collection, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions 
used; (c) Evaluate ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of 
the information to be collected; and (d) Minimize the reporting burden 
on those who are to respond, including the use of automated collection 
techniques or other forms of information technology.
    Comments that you submit in response to this notice are a matter of 
public record. We will include, or summarize, each comment in our 
request to OMB to approve this ICR. Before including your address, 
phone number, email address, or other personal identifying information 
in your comment, you should be aware that your entire comment--
including your personal identifying information--may be made publicly 
available at any time. While you may ask us in your comment to withhold 
your personal identifying information from public review, we cannot 
guarantee that we will be able to do so.

Sheleen Dumas,
Departmental PRA Compliance Officer, Office of the Under Secretary for 
Economic Affairs, Commerce Department.

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP)
Description: The Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP) is a nationally representative longitudinal survey that provides comprehensive information on the dynamics of income, employment, household composition, and government program participation. SIPP is also a leading source of data on economic well-being, family dynamics, education, wealth, health insurance, child care, and food security. The survey interviews individuals for several years and provides monthly data about changes in household and family composition and economic circumstances over time.
URL: https://census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp.html

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research the SIPP dataset from multiple angles. Let me start with the main Census page and some broad searches.I have good foundational material. Now let me dig deeper into the current design, the 2014/2021 redesigns, data access, and users.Good progress. Let me check recent news (2025 budget threats, program status), linked-data products, and public benefit statistics.The search tool hit its limit, but I can still fetch pages directly. Let me pull the Wikipedia article and the Census history page for final details.# Research Report: Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP)

**Verification note:** The title, description, and URL you provided are accurate and match the U.S. Census Bureau's official program page (census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp.html) essentially verbatim. The description appears on the Census Bureau's "About This Survey" page. This report is compiled from Census Bureau documentation, National Academies assessments, and supporting sources.

---

## 1. Overview and Publisher

- **Publisher / Steward:** U.S. Census Bureau, an agency of the Department of Commerce. Within Census, SIPP is housed under the demographic surveys programs (Social, Economic, and Housing Statistics Division).
- **Type:** A nationally representative **longitudinal household panel survey** — the federal government's principal source of *monthly* data on the dynamics of income, employment, household composition, and participation in government transfer programs.
- **Program URL:** https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp.html
- **Mission statement (Census):** to provide a nationally representative sample for evaluating (1) annual and sub-annual income dynamics; (2) movements into and out of government transfer programs; (3) the family and social context of individuals and households; and (4) interactions among these areas.
- **Geographic scope / population:** Civilian, noninstitutionalized U.S. population (individuals 15+ and others living with them).

## 2. Legal Authority and Mandate

- **Core statute:** Title 13, United States Code, **Section 182**, which authorizes the Secretary of Commerce to conduct surveys collecting statistics on income, employment, and related topics. The Census Bureau explicitly states it sponsors SIPP "under the authority of Title 13, United States Code, Section 182."
- **Confidentiality authority:** Title 13 §9(a) (statistical-use-only, no identifying publications, sworn-officer access), §23(c), and §214 (penalties for unauthorized disclosure — up to 5 years' imprisonment and a $250,000 fine, as strengthened by CIPSEA and the Foundations of Evidence-Based Policymaking Act of 2018).
- **Survey clearance:** SIPP operates under the Paperwork Reduction Act and must obtain OMB clearance for each panel (OMB control numbers in the 0607-xxxx series; e.g., the 2018 panel's supporting statements show detailed burden and sample-design justifications submitted to OMB).
- **Congressional mandate (indirect):** SIPP's continuation has repeatedly been shaped by Congress — most notably after the 2006 attempted termination, when Congress directed the Census Bureau "to work with stakeholders to reengineer SIPP to develop a more accurate and timely survey to capture the economic dynamics of the country" (National Academies, *The 2014 Redesign of the Survey of Income and Program Participation: An Assessment*).

## 3. History

**Origins (1975–1983).** SIPP grew out of the Income Survey Development Program (ISDP), initiated in 1975 by the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare (HEW) in collaboration with Census, to fix known weaknesses of the March Current Population Survey income supplement: underreporting of property income, misreporting of program participation, and lack of monthly detail and eligibility information. National tests in 1978 (~2,000 households) and 1979 (~8,200 households) followed. Funding was deleted from the budget in 1980 and 1981; a rescue effort in 1982 restored funding, and the first interviews took place in **October 1983** with over 20,000 households.

**Classic panel era (1984–1993 panels).** New panels launched each February with overlapping samples (roughly 12,400–23,600 households), each interviewed every 4 months over 32 months. There have been **17 SIPP panels since 1984**.

**1990 CNSTAT review → 1996 redesign.** A National Research Council/Committee on National Statistics review (Citro and Kalton, *The Future of the Survey of Income and Program Participation*) led to the 1996 Panel redesign: a larger sample, 4-year (48-month) coverage, computer-assisted interviewing (CAI), and oversampling of high-poverty areas. Fielding was delayed by the 1995–96 government shutdowns; mid-panel, Congress passed PRWORA (welfare reform, AFDC→TANF), forcing Census to adapt program questions on the fly — an early demonstration of SIPP's policy-relevance.

**2006 near-death experience.** In 2006 Census announced SIPP would be terminated and replaced by the "Dynamics of Economic Well-Being System" (DEWS). An intensive user-community campaign (letter-writing, lobbying, media) reversed the decision; SIPP was reinstated with a 2008 panel (~45,000 households), DEWS was abandoned, and Congress mandated the reengineering effort.

**2014 re-engineering.** The 2014 Panel introduced a fundamentally new design: **annual interviews** (instead of every 4 months) with a 12-month calendar-year reference period, an **event history calendar** collection method, dependent interviewing, and consolidated content (replacing the old "core + topical module" structure).

**2018–present: overlapping panel design.** Beginning with the 2018 Panel, Census adopted **overlapping annual panels** (a return to a pre-1996 concept), fielding a new panel each year and interviewing multiple panels concurrently. Key recent facts:
- The 2019 Panel was discontinued after Wave 1 due to low response.
- Data products are now named by **calendar year of collection** (e.g., "2025 SIPP" = data collected in 2025 covering calendar year 2024); the Census Bureau recommends combining all panels covering the same reference period for key estimates.
- The 2021 Panel Wave 1 achieved ~42% household-level participation; the combined CY2021 release (2018 W4 + 2020 W2 + 2021 W1) had a cross-sectional weighted response rate of **48.8%** (~24,000 households, ~56,500 person interviews) — reflecting the sharp, industry-wide decline in survey response.

## 4. Content and Methodology (what's in the data)

- **Coverage:** Detailed income by source (earnings, asset income, transfers — dozens of program-specific sources including TANF, SNAP, SSI, SSDI, unemployment insurance, Medicaid/Medicare, WIC, housing assistance); employment and job spells; household and family composition; **wealth and assets** (a signature strength — detailed net worth); health insurance coverage; disability; education; child care and child support; marital/fertility/migration histories; and food security. COVID-19 content was added to the 2021 collection.
- **Unit and structure:** Public-use files are **person-month level** (up to 12 records per person per year in the 2014+ design), with household, person, spell, and monthly variable types, plus ID variables for longitudinal linking.
- **Weights:** Cross-sectional person-month weights, **replicate weights** (240 in the 2025 release) for variance estimation, and separate longitudinal weight files for 2-, 3-, and 4-year cohorts, with nonresponse and poststratification adjustments.
- **Complex design caveat:** SIPP uses multistage stratified sampling; standard software assuming simple random samples will understate standard errors — users must use replicate weights or specialized software (e.g., SAS/Stata/R survey procedures).
- **Known data-quality issues** (important for users):
  - **Seam bias** — changes disproportionately reported at the boundary between reference periods; mitigated since 2004 by dependent interviewing (which roughly halved the effect in many topics).
  - **Attrition** in longitudinal panels.
  - **Recall error, time-in-sample effects, and underreporting** of income and program benefits relative to administrative records (documented in SSA/Census match studies).
  - **Disclosure-avoidance edits** (topcoding/bottomcoding, perturbation, geographic suppression) mean public-use estimates can differ slightly from Census-published statistics.

## 5. Typical Users and Uses

**Federal agencies (documented by the National Academies assessment of six heavy user agencies):**
- **Social Security Administration** — the most intensive user: describing beneficiary populations, and microsimulation via the **MINT** (Modeling Income in the Near Term) and **FEM** (Financial Eligibility Model) models, built on SIPP matched to SSA administrative records (earnings, benefit, and Numident files) to evaluate OASDI/SSI reform proposals.
- **Congressional Budget Office** — simulation models for budget and program analysis.
- **USDA Food and Nutrition Service and Economic Research Service** — SNAP eligibility/participation analysis, including the MATH SIPP+ model (Mathematica) and linked administrative SNAP studies.
- **HHS/ASPE** and others for welfare-program evaluation and economic well-being statistics.

**Academic and research community:** A National Academies literature review identified **638 unique works using SIPP between 2000 and 2014 across 26 topic areas**. SIPP underpins research on poverty dynamics and program entry/exit, wealth inequality, health insurance coverage transitions, disability, child well-being, marriage and family structure, and labor-market dynamics (e.g., minimum-wage employment studies such as Clemens & Wither 2019).

**Other users:** journalists and policy advocates tracking program effectiveness; state and local analysts; think tanks; microsimulation modelers; students. The 2006 rescue campaign demonstrates that SIPP has an unusually organized and invested user community.

## 6. Benefits to the Public

1. **Evidence-based policy:** The only federal dataset providing *monthly, longitudinal* detail on how households move into and out of programs and poverty — enabling evaluation of program eligibility rules, benefit adequacy, welfare reform, and proposed reforms *before* enactment.
2. **Cost forecasting:** Feeds the models SSA, CBO, and USDA use to project program costs and coverage.
3. **Measuring what annual snapshots miss:** Monthly income dynamics, short poverty spells, insurance coverage gaps, and wealth detail far richer than the CPS or ACS.
4. **Free, open public data:** All microdata back to the 1984 panel are freely downloadable with no licensing restrictions (U.S. federal government works; public domain).
5. **Linked-data innovation:** SIPP pioneered census–administrative data linkage (SSA/IRS matched files) and synthetic data products (see below), expanding what researchers can learn about economic well-being without exposing confidential records.

## 7. Data Access and Products (data librarian / data scientist notes)

- **Public-use microdata (PUF):** Available from https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/data/datasets.html — current releases (2018–2025) and historical panels (1984–2014). Formats: **SAS, Stata, and pipe-delimited text** (.zip archives), with data dictionaries, schemas, and Python/R/Stata input examples. 2025 SIPP covers reference period Jan–Dec 2024.
- **API:** SIPP microdata are available through the **Census Microdata API** (api.census.gov/data/{year}/sipp), with variables documented in HTML/XML/JSON.
- **Online tools:** Census Microdata Access Tool (MDAT) at data.census.gov (beta; Census warns users to understand SIPP universing before tabulating).
- **Restricted access:** Raw (unedited, identified, and linked) SIPP data — including matches to SSA earnings/benefit records, IRS W-2s, and other administrative data — are available via approved projects at **Federal Statistical Research Data Centers (FSRDCs)**.
- **Synthetic/linked products:** The **SIPP Synthetic Beta (SSB)** integrates SIPP person records with SSA and IRS administrative data, synthesized to preserve confidentiality (developed with Cornell, SSA, IRS).
- **Documentation:** Annual Users' Guides, Source & Accuracy Statements, nonresponse bias reports, questionnaires, and release notes/errata are all on the technical documentation pages.
- **Third-party distribution:** Historical SIPP files have been mirrored/archived by ICPSR and NBER; the Census Bureau remains the authoritative source.

## 8. Preservationist Notes

- **Continuity of record:** 40+ years of continuous panel data (1984–present), one of the longest-running longitudinal income datasets in the world; breaks in the series design (1996, 2014, 2018) require bridge documentation, which Census has provided (e.g., 2014-vs-2018 income recode alignment notes).
- **Funding fragility is a recurring theme:** defunded 1980–81, nearly terminated in 2006, disrupted by government shutdowns (1995–96), hit by declining response rates (2019 panel abandoned after one wave). Anyone depending on SIPP longitudinally should monitor appropriations and the annual OMB clearance process.
- **Disclosure-avoidance evolution:** A 2024 National Academies report (*A Roadmap for Disclosure Avoidance in SIPP*) flags future modernization of confidentiality protection (including discussion of differential-privacy-style approaches) — a potential reproducibility/preservation concern for time-series research, since methods could change across waves.
- **Citation and identifiers:** data.census.gov and the SIPP datasets page serve as canonical landing pages; the program is consistently catalogued as a Census demographic survey program (DCD/SEHSD).

## 9. Notable Cautions for the Four Personas (summary)

| Persona | Key takeaways |
|---|---|
| **Preservationist** | 17 panels since 1984; multiple design regimes (1984–93, 1996–2013, 2014–17, 2018+); panel-termination and defunding precedents; errata and re-releases happen (check release notes). |
| **Data librarian** | Free PUFs in SAS/Stata/CSV; API and MDAT; excellent Users' Guides; name conventions changed (panel/wave vs. calendar year of collection) — explain this to patrons. |
| **Data scientist** | Person-month structure, complex survey design, replicate + longitudinal weights, seam bias, underreporting vs. admin data, topcoding edits, FSRDC path for linked data. |
| **Policy activist** | Statutory basis (13 U.S.C. §182) and congressional direction post-2006; feeds SSA MINT/FEM, CBO, and USDA models; the definitive public evidence base on program entry/exit and poverty dynamics; history shows organized advocacy can save it. |

## 10. Primary Sources Consulted

- Census Bureau SIPP program, About, FAQs, History pages (census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/…)
- 2021–2025 SIPP Users' Guides and Source & Accuracy Statements (www2.census.gov)
- National Academies: *The 2014 Redesign of SIPP: An Assessment* (2018); *A Roadmap for Disclosure Avoidance in SIPP* (2024)
- OMB supporting statements for the 2018 SIPP Panel (omb.report)
- Institute for Research on Poverty, *Focus* article on SIPP's history; Wikipedia entry (history/authority)
- Census SIPP Synthetic Beta guidance page; Census Microdata API documentation

One gap I could not verify because of search-tool limits: whether any budget actions in 2024–2025 have affected SIPP's fielding schedule or future panels. Given SIPP's history of budget brushes with death, I'd recommend checking the Census Bureau budget justifications and the SIPP "Data" page before relying on a specific future release year.

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

**Bottom line up front:** SIPP is in the middle of an unprecedented, administration-driven restructuring. The historical archive is fully intact and the most recent release came out on schedule, but the FY2026 President's Budget proposes a deep cut targeting SIPP specifically, the Census Bureau has announced that **the 2027 national collection will be skipped** in favor of a redesigned field test, and the Bureau has lost significant staff and leadership. ## Category 1: Historical Data Availability

**Evidence gathered:**
- The Census Bureau SIPP datasets page (verified live, Oct. 2026) states: "Access SIPP data by year (2018–2025) or panel/wave (1984–2014)" — the full 40-year archive of public-use files remains posted, including the 2025 SIPP primary file, replicate weights, and complete technical documentation back to 1984. ([census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/data/datasets.html](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/data/datasets.html))
- The 2025 SIPP release (July 15, 2026) shipped with full accompanying documentation: Users' Guide, Source & Accuracy Statement, crosswalks to 2024 variables, and an interactive codebook. ([Census press release CB26-TPS.41](https://www.census.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2026/2025-sipp.html))
- No reports of SIPP files being removed from census.gov or data.census.gov; historical files also remain mirrored at ICPSR and NBER, providing redundancy.
- Minor caveat (pre-dating 2025): the SIPP Synthetic Beta (a linked/synthetic derivative product) was retired earlier, but that was a separate product, not the core microdata.

**Assessment: No Known Issue.** All historical data from 1984–2025 remain publicly accessible with no known alterations, and third-party archival copies exist.

## Category 2: Future Data Availability

**Evidence gathered:**
- *On-time publication (mitigating):* The 2025 SIPP (reference year 2024) was released July 15, 2026 — consistent with the recent cadence (July 2024 and July 2023 releases). The annual release schedule has held. ([2025 SIPP Users' Guide release table](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/tech-documentation/methodology/2025_SIPP_Users_Guide.pdf))
- *Skipped collection (aggravating — decisive):* A Federal Register notice of Aug. 7, 2026 (91 FR 51147) states the Census Bureau "plans to request clearance from OMB for a **field test** of SIPP in calendar year 2027. **This collection will be in lieu of a national collection** using the questionnaires, systems, and processes in place since 2014." The field test sample is only ~6,000 respondents (vs. 40,000 in the current panel ICR), with comments due Oct. 6, 2026. ([Federal Register 2026-16188](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/08/07/2026-16188/agency-information-collection-activities-submission-to-the-office-of-management-and-budget-omb-for))
- *ICR status:* The current ICR (OMB 0607-1000, "2024 SIPP Panel") is Active but **expires 12/31/2026**. The pending new ICR covers only the field test — there is currently no approved ICR for a national collection after 2026. ([reginfo.gov](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAViewICR?ref_nbr=202310-0607-005); [omb.report/omb/0607-1000](https://omb.report/omb/0607-1000))
- *Budget:* The FY2026 President's Budget cuts the Current Surveys account ~$40M (12.3%) "primarily target[ing]" SIPP, proposing SIPP "transition to a more effective approach that merges modern survey techniques with advanced data science methods" — and the CBJ "does not outline SIPP's potential transition nor clarify if the program will continue under its current name." ([The Census Project, 6/30/2025](https://thecensusproject.org/2025/06/30/department-of-commerce-releases-fiscal-year-2026-census-budget-details/); CRS IF13105)
- *Operational disruption:* The Oct. 2025 government shutdown triggered "lack of funds" RIF notices; hiring freezes and a 3,000+ item contract-approval backlog have slowed Census operations generally. ([Bloomberg Law](https://news.bloomberglaw.com/daily-labor-report/census-bureau-hit-with-layoffs-as-100-get-notices-in-shutdown); [AMSTAT](https://www.amstat.org/docs/default-source/amstat-documents/the-nations-data-at-risk-2025/census.pdf))

**Assessment: High Risk.** A national collection cycle is being skipped (2027), the existing national-collection ICR expires at the end of 2026 with no successor national ICR in process, and the program's continuation "under its current name" is explicitly unresolved in the budget request. This squarely meets the "collection or publication skipped" criterion. It is not "Gone" because data collection/publication has not been terminated: the 2025 release occurred on time, 2026 collection proceeds under the active ICR, and the Bureau describes the field test as "an important step toward building the modern program" — a redesign, not an abolition (at least as of Oct. 2026).

## Category 3: Data Quality

**Evidence gathered:**
- *Realized reduction in sample size:* New-panel sample sizes have collapsed: 2018 Panel: 44,870 households; 2020: 22,241; 2022: 33,302; 2023: 13,293; 2024: 12,266; **2025: 11,743** — a ~74% reduction in new-panel sample since 2018, directly reducing statistical power and granularity. ([2025 SIPP Users' Guide](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/tech-documentation/methodology/2025_SIPP_Users_Guide.pdf))
- *Planned further reductions:* The FY2026 budget proposes "a smaller, more targeted sample while utilizing non-survey data." The redesigned instrument uses a **six-month reference period** (down from 12 months) and web-first self-response with limited in-person follow-up. (Federal Register 91 FR 51147; The Census Project)
- *Response rates:* The CY2021 combined release had a weighted household response rate of 48.8%, and the 2019 panel was abandoned after one wave due to low response — pre-existing quality pressures the redesign is meant to address.
- *Neutral/mitigating:* The Bureau claims the redesign will "enhance both the timeliness and accuracy of statistical outputs"; documentation quality of recent releases remains high. A multimode redesign also predates the current administration (testing via HTOPS began in late 2024), so not all change is politically driven.
- *Stakeholder reaction:* NPR's Hansi Lo Wang reported the Bureau "is planning to scale back" SIPP — used to measure SNAP and other program use — "and start using 'non-survey data' to lower costs."

**Assessment: High Risk.** Reductions in granularity have already occurred (dramatic sample shrinkage) and further reductions are formally planned (smaller targeted sample, shortened reference period, mode change). Whether the redesign ultimately improves timeliness is speculative; the granularity loss is concrete.

## Category 4: Statutory Context

**Evidence gathered:**
- *Explicit authorization:* SIPP operates under Title 13, U.S.C., Sections 141 and 182 — explicitly cited in the current ICR and Federal Register notices. Census describes itself as conducting SIPP "under the authority of Title 13, Section 182." Authorization is not vague.
- *Not statutorily mandated:* No statute requires SIPP to be conducted; unlike the decennial census or ACS, Congress mandates no SIPP publication deadlines. Its 2006 near-termination was administratively proposed.
- *Heavy programmatic use with no true substitute:* SSA (MINT and FEM microsimulation models for OASDI/SSI policy), CBO, USDA/FNS (SNAP eligibility and cost modeling), and HHS/ASPE depend on SIPP's monthly longitudinal program-participation dynamics. No other federal survey (CPS, ACS) collects monthly, multi-year longitudinal income/program-transition data; the 2018 National Academies assessment documented six heavy user agencies.
- *Administration's substitution claim:* The FY2026 budget asserts "non-survey data" and "advanced data science methods" can replace much of SIPP's content — an assertion of substitutability, though no operational substitute currently exists.

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** SIPP is not statutorily required, but its authorization is explicitly named, it is essential to the analytical implementation of major federal programs (Social Security, SNAP), and no existing alternative collection can substitute for its longitudinal dynamics. This fits the Moderate profile. The High profile would require vague authorization, real substitutes, or no programmatic use — none of which hold today, though the Administration's administrative-data substitution claim is a worrying indicator that could push this to High if a "substitute" product actually materializes.

## Category 5: Staffing and Funding

**Evidence gathered:**
- *Staffing:* The Census Bureau "has lost an estimated 15% in staffing since FY24" (AMSTAT). AFGE reports ~1,500 Census workers departed since January 2025 via the deferred resignation program, plus 100 reduction-in-force notices issued Oct. 10, 2025 at the Tucson call center during the shutdown. Department of Commerce fired 762 employees beginning Feb. 27, 2025 (later subject to reinstatement litigation). At least five division/office chiefs left in early 2025, including staff tied to the Data Stewardship committee. ([AMSTAT "The Nation's Data at Risk 2025"](https://www.amstat.org/docs/default-source/amstat-documents/the-nations-data-at-risk-2025/census.pdf); [Bloomberg Law](https://news.bloomberglaw.com/daily-labor-report/census-bureau-hit-with-layoffs-as-100-get-notices-in-shutdown); [NPR, 4/17/2025](https://www.npr.org/2025/04/17/nx-s1-5349435/us-census-bureau-data-decennial))
- *Funding:* FY2025 budget held flat at $1.385B (a real purchasing-power cut of ~2.4%). The FY2026 President's Budget requests $73M for Current Demographic Statistics vs. $113M enacted in FY2024/FY2025 — a **$40M (~35%) cut to the SIPP-anchored account**. SIPP itself cost roughly $48M/year (per Census Project FY2023 figures), so the requested cut approaches the program's entire historical budget. (CRS IF13105; The Census Project)
- *Leadership:* No Senate-confirmed director; political appointee George Cook named acting director in September 2025 after serving as acting Under Secretary. The FY2026 budget also proposes reorganizing Census, BLS, and BEA under a consolidated Commerce structure. An OIG evaluation found the Bureau lacks strategies to address field-representative staffing gaps. (AMSTAT; NPR)
- *Caveat:* I could not verify the final enacted FY2026 appropriation (the Oct. 2025 shutdown and continuing resolutions complicate this; the search tool's result cap prevented confirmation), so the $40M cut may remain a *request* rather than enacted law. The staffing losses, however, are documented facts.

**Assessment: High Risk.** Multiple High Risk thresholds are met: 1,000+ staff lost (~1,500+ departures plus RIFs), estimated 15% agency staffing loss, a proposed budget cut to SIPP's account far exceeding 20%, and leadership change (acting political-appointee director, departed division chiefs). Even if Congress softens the FY2026 appropriation, the staffing losses alone sustain High Risk.

## Category 6: Policy

**Evidence gathered:**
- *Administration-driven restructuring:* The FY2026 President's Budget (released June 25, 2025) singles out SIPP for "major changes," criticizing its data collection as "expensive and challenging for respondents," and proposes shifting to non-survey/administrative data — explicitly aligned with the Administration's government-efficiency and data-modernization priorities. (The Census Project)
- *Significant change already in motion:* The Aug. 2026 Federal Register notice implements that direction — 2027 will bring a field test in lieu of the national collection, with a web-first, smaller-sample, shorter-reference-period design, following a summer 2026 internet self-response test. This is not merely "proposed or pending"; the field tests are underway and the national-collection skip is scheduled. (91 FR 51147)
- *Broader context:* Presidential memorandum on excluding undocumented immigrants from the census count; proposed reorganization of the statistical agencies under Commerce; cancellation of other Census collections (e.g., a 2026 survey of local governments) with alternatives cited; delayed pulse-survey collections. SIPP's subject matter — government program participation (SNAP, TANF, SSI) — intersects with areas where the Administration has pursued spending cuts, which stakeholders view as raising the salience of its data.
- *Counterpoint:* SIPP modernization research (multimode, self-response) began before January 2025 under prior leadership, and the 2025 data release proceeded normally. The Census Bureau's own notice frames the changes as methodological improvement ("critical" testing toward "the modern program"), not a negative policy note.

**Assessment: High Risk.** The rubric's High level includes "other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities," and that describes the current situation precisely: a President's Budget-driven scale-back of a named survey, replacement of a national collection cycle with a field test, and substitution of survey content with administrative data — changes that journalists and stakeholder organizations characterize as scale-backs of a key program-participation dataset. This is well beyond the "proposed or pending" (Moderate) stage, but short of "Gone" since collection and publication continue in transition.

## Caveats on evidence limitations

1. I could not confirm the enacted FY2026 appropriation outcome (whether Congress accepted or rejected the $40M SIPP cut) due to the search tool's result cap; the government shutdown that began Oct. 2025 and continuing-resolution funding make this genuinely uncertain.
2. The USAJobs staffing tracker (usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com) is a JavaScript application scheduled for archiving on Dec. 31, 2025; its data could not be directly extracted, so staffing figures rely on AMSTAT, AFGE/Bloomberg Law, and NPR reporting instead.
3. Whether a 2026 SIPP panel launched in February 2026 under the existing ICR (which covers panels through its 12/31/2026 expiration) is not directly confirmed in my sources; the 2025 Users' Guide table shows the 2023, 2024, and 2025 panels as "Ongoing" but was published before Feb. 2026.

## Summary of Risk Levels

**Historical Data Availability: No Known Issue**
— Full 1984–2025 archive intact and publicly posted, with third-party redundancy.

**Future Data Availability: High Risk**
— 2025 release on time, but the 2027 national collection is being skipped in favor of a field test, and no national-collection ICR exists beyond 12/31/2026.

**Data Quality: High Risk**
— New-panel sample sizes down ~74% since 2018, with a planned smaller targeted sample and shortened (6-month) reference period.

**Statutory Context: Moderate Risk**
— Explicit authorization (13 U.S.C. §§141, 182) but no statutory mandate; heavy programmatic use and no existing substitute, though the Administration asserts administrative-data alternatives.

**Staffing and Funding: High Risk**
— ~1,500+ staff departures, ~15% staffing loss, proposed ~$40M cut targeting SIPP, and leadership turnover (acting political-appointee director).

**Policy: High Risk**
— President's Budget-driven restructuring and scheduled collection skip aligned with Administration priorities; field tests already underway.

**Overall preservationist recommendation:** This is a dataset whose *archive* is safe today but whose *future stream* is at genuine risk of a series break. Anyone with long-term dependence on SIPP should (1) archive the complete 1984–2025 public-use files now (they are free, public-domain downloads); (2) monitor the OMB docket for ICR 0607-1000 and the 2027 field-test ICR outcome; (3) track the FY2026/FY2027 appropriations conference language on SIPP; and (4) watch whether the 2026 panel's later waves (needed for longitudinal continuity into reference year 2026+) are actually fielded.
